To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

conversational programmers are a class of learners that do not have to write code, but still want to learn programming, and modern learning resources fail them in their pursuit of improving their participation in technical discussions.

(1) conversational programmers have a mismatch of expectations with modern learning resources that are not designed with their goals in mind, (2) conversational programmers are often not able to find the appropriate resources to learn the skills they need to participate in technical conversations, (3) conversational programmers often have to rely on resources that are not learner-centric, and (4) conversational programmers do not always find the right resources to learn the technical skills they need to be able to participate in technical discussions

Conversational programmers represent an understudied class of learners who do not write code, yet try learn programming to improve participation in technical conversations and are often frustrated by modern learning resources that focus on programming syntax and logical constructs.
